title: Custom Exception Hierarchy
objective: Define base AppError and subclasses ValidationError and AuthError.
description:
Task: Build your own exception classes, so one except clause can catch a whole family of errors.
• class AppError(Exception) with a class attribute code = 500
• class ValidationError(AppError) with code = 400
• class AuthError(AppError) with code = 401

Write a class UserStore that keeps usernames and passwords:
• register(self, user, pwd): raise ValidationError('password too short') if pwd has fewer than 6 characters, raise ValidationError('user exists') if the user is already registered, otherwise store the user
• login(self, user, pwd): raise AuthError('invalid credentials') if the user is unknown or the password is wrong

Commands:
• REGISTER user pwd → print REGISTERED user
• LOGIN user pwd → print WELCOME user
• For both commands, catch AppError (the BASE class) and print <ClassName>[<code>]: <message>, for example ValidationError[400]: user exists

Example: REGISTER asha secret1, LOGIN asha nope prints REGISTERED asha and AuthError[401]: invalid credentials.
input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
output_format: One output line for every command, as described.
constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
User names and passwords are words without spaces
sample_input_1:
2
REGISTER asha secret1
LOGIN asha nope
hint_1: class ValidationError(AppError): code = 400 is a complete class: it inherits everything else from AppError.
hint_2: except AppError as e: also catches ValidationError and AuthError, because they are subclasses.
hint_3: type(e).__name__ gives the class name, and e.code finds the class attribute of the subclass.

title: Vehicle Hierarchy with Super
objective: Implement Vehicle base and Car subclass extending __init__ via super().
time_complexity: O(1) per command, O(N) per LIST
description:
Task: Write three classes that build on each other with super():
• Vehicle: __init__(self, make, model, year) stores the three values. Class attribute wheels = 0. describe(self) returns '<year> <make> <model>'
• Car(Vehicle): __init__(self, make, model, year, doors) calls super().__init__(make, model, year) and stores doors. Class attribute wheels = 4. describe(self) returns super().describe() + ' (<doors> doors)'
• ElectricCar(Car): __init__(self, make, model, year, doors, kwh) calls super().__init__(...) and stores kwh. describe(self) returns super().describe() + ' [<kwh> kWh]'

Commands:
• VEHICLE make model year, CAR make model year doors, ECAR make model year doors kwh → create the object and keep it in a list (prints nothing)
• LIST → print describe() of every object in creation order
• INFO i → for the object at index i (from 0) print: <ClassName>, wheels=<wheels>, is Car: <True/False>. Use isinstance(obj, Car)

Example: CAR Toyota Corolla 2020 4 then LIST prints 2020 Toyota Corolla (4 doors).
input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description). INFO always uses a valid index.
output_format: LIST prints one line per object; INFO prints one line. Create commands print nothing.
constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
Makes and models are words without spaces
year, doors and kwh are integers
hint_1: super().__init__(make, model, year) lets Vehicle set the shared attributes, so Car does not repeat that code.
hint_2: ElectricCar inherits wheels = 4 from Car without writing it again.
hint_3: isinstance(obj, Car) is True for an ElectricCar too, because ElectricCar is a subclass of Car.

title: Dataclass with Ordering
objective: Implement @dataclass(order=True) for items comparing by price.
description:
Task: The dataclasses module writes __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and, with order=True, also <, <=, > and >= for you.

Write a dataclass Item:
@dataclass(order=True)
class Item:
price: float
name: str

Comparisons use the fields in the order they are written: first price, then name (only when the prices are equal).

Commands:
• ADD name price → create an Item and keep it in a list (prints nothing)
• SORTED → print the items from cheapest to most expensive, one per line, using repr (the dataclass repr, like Item(price=2.5, name='pen'))
• CHEAPEST → print min(items) using repr
• COMPARE i j → compare the items at indexes i and j (from 0) and print <, == or >

Example: ADD pen 2.5, ADD book 12.0, CHEAPEST prints Item(price=2.5, name='pen').
input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description). SORTED, CHEAPEST and COMPARE are only used when the list has the items they need.
output_format: SORTED prints one line per item; CHEAPEST and COMPARE print one line. ADD prints nothing.
constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
Names are words without spaces
0 <= price <= 10^6
sample_input_2:
4
ADD b 5
ADD a 5
SORTED
COMPARE 0 1
hint_1: from dataclasses import dataclass, then put @dataclass(order=True) on the line above class Item.
hint_2: Create items with Item(float(price), name): the fields come in the order they are declared.
hint_3: sorted(items) and min(items) work directly, because order=True gives the class comparison methods.

title: Employee Payroll Polymorphism
objective: Base Employee with Salaried and Hourly polymorphic earnings.
description:
Task: Polymorphism means different classes answer the same method call in their own way.

Write a base class and two subclasses:
• Employee: __init__(self, name). monthly_pay(self) raises NotImplementedError, because a plain Employee has no pay rule
• Salaried(Employee): __init__(self, name, annual). monthly_pay returns annual / 12
• Hourly(Employee): __init__(self, name, rate, hours). monthly_pay returns rate * hours for the first 160 hours, plus 1.5 * rate for every hour above 160

Commands:
• SALARIED name annual, HOURLY name rate hours → create the employee (prints nothing)
• PAYROLL → print one line per employee in creation order: <name> (<ClassName>): <pay with 2 decimals>, then a last line TOTAL: <sum with 2 decimals>. The loop must just call e.monthly_pay() for every employee, without checking the type

Example: SALARIED asha 60000, HOURLY ben 20 170, PAYROLL prints
asha (Salaried): 5000.00
ben (Hourly): 3500.00
TOTAL: 8500.00
input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
output_format: For every PAYROLL: one line per employee, then the TOTAL line.
hint_2: Overtime hours are max(0, hours - 160); normal hours are min(hours, 160).
hint_3: The PAYROLL loop calls employee.monthly_pay() and Python picks the right version for each object.

title: Payment Gateway Polymorphism
objective: Abstract PaymentGateway with CreditCard, UPI, and Crypto classes.
description:
Task: An abstract class describes what every subclass must provide, and cannot be created itself.

Write the classes using the abc module:
• PaymentGateway(ABC) with an abstract method fee(self, amount), and a normal method pay(self, amount) that returns (amount + fee, fee)
• CreditCard: fee = 2.9% of the amount + 0.30
• UPI: fee = 0
• Crypto: fee = 1.00 + 1% of the amount

Commands:
• PAY method amount → method is CARD, UPI or CRYPTO. Print <ClassName>: charged <total> (fee <fee>), both with 2 decimals. If the amount <= 0 print INVALID AMOUNT. If the method is unknown print UNKNOWN METHOD
• ABSTRACT → try to create PaymentGateway() directly. Python raises TypeError because it has an abstract method: catch it and print CANNOT INSTANTIATE PaymentGateway

Example: PAY CARD 100 prints CreditCard: charged 103.20 (fee 3.20).
input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
output_format: One output line for every command, as described.
hint_1: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod; put @abstractmethod above def fee.
hint_2: Keep a dictionary {'CARD': CreditCard(), 'UPI': UPI(), 'CRYPTO': Crypto()} to pick the gateway.
hint_3: pay() is written once in the base class and calls self.fee(amount), which runs the subclass version.

title: Shape Geometry Polymorphism
objective: Base Shape with Circle and Polygon computing polymorphic area.
description:
Task: Write a base class Shape and two subclasses:
• Shape: area(self) raises NotImplementedError
• Circle(Shape): __init__(self, r); area = math.pi * r * r
• Polygon(Shape): __init__(self, points) with a list of (x, y) tuples. If there are fewer than 3 points, raise ValueError('polygon needs at least 3 points'). Area with the shoelace formula: abs(sum of x[i] * y[i+1] - x[i+1] * y[i] over all i, wrapping around to the first point) / 2

Commands:
• CIRCLE r → add a circle (prints nothing)
• POLYGON x1 y1 x2 y2 ... → add a polygon. If it raises ValueError, print INVALID: <message> and do not add it
• LIST → one line per shape in the order added: <ClassName>: <area with 2 decimals>
• TOTAL → the sum of all areas with 2 decimals
• LARGEST → <ClassName>: <area> of the shape with the biggest area (the first one on a tie), or NONE if there are no shapes

Example: CIRCLE 1, POLYGON 0 0 4 0 4 3, LIST prints Circle: 3.14 and Polygon: 6.00.
input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
output_format: One line for every TOTAL, LARGEST and rejected POLYGON; one line per shape for every LIST.
sample_output_2:
INVALID: polygon needs at least 3 points
NONE
hint_1: Pair the coordinates with zip: list(zip(nums[0::2], nums[1::2])).
hint_2: In the shoelace sum, the next point of the last point is the first one: points[(i + 1) % n].
hint_3: max(shapes, key=lambda s: s.area()) returns the first shape with the largest area.

title: Sequence Magic Methods
objective: Implement __len__ and __getitem__ to enable indexing and slicing.
time_complexity: O(1) per GET, O(K) per SLICE
description:
Task: When a class defines __len__ and __getitem__, Python lets you use len(obj), obj[i] and obj[a:b] on it, like on a list.

Write a class SongList that wraps a list of song names:
• __init__(self, songs=None) stores a copy of the list (an empty list when songs is None)
• add(self, song) appends a song
• __len__(self) returns the number of songs
• __getitem__(self, index): if index is a slice object, return a NEW SongList with the selected songs; otherwise return the song at that index. A bad index raises IndexError by itself
• __repr__(self) returns SongList(<list of songs>)

Commands:
• ADD song → add a song (the song name is one word; prints nothing)
• LEN → print len(songs)
• GET i → print songs[i], or INDEX ERROR if it raises IndexError
• SLICE a b [step] → print repr(songs[a:b]) or repr(songs[a:b:step]) when a step is given

Example: ADD a, ADD b, ADD c, GET -1, SLICE 0 2 prints c and SongList(['a', 'b']).

Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
output_format: One output line for every LEN, GET and SLICE command.

ADD b
ADD c
GET -1
SLICE 0 2
hint_1: isinstance(index, slice) tells you whether obj[a:b] was used.
hint_2: self.songs[index] already understands both ints and slices; just wrap a slice result in SongList(...).
hint_3: Python turns songs[0:2] into songs.__getitem__(slice(0, 2, None)).

title: Value Equality & Hashing
objective: Implement __eq__ and __hash__ for hash table compatibility in sets/dicts.
description:
Task: By default two objects are equal only if they are the SAME object. To use objects as set items or dict keys by their VALUE, a class needs __eq__ and a matching __hash__: equal objects must have equal hashes.

Write a class Point:
• __init__(self, x, y)
• __eq__(self, other): True when other is a Point with the same x and y. For anything else return NotImplemented
• __hash__(self): return hash((self.x, self.y))
• __repr__(self): Point(x, y)

Commands:
• ADD x y → add Point(x, y) to a set. Print ADDED, or DUPLICATE if an equal point is already there
• HAS x y → print True or False (is an equal point in the set?)
• COUNT → print the size of the set
• LABEL x y name → store name in a dict under the key Point(x, y) (a new name replaces the old one; prints nothing)
• NAME x y → print the label of Point(x, y), or NONE

Example: ADD 1 2, ADD 1 2, COUNT prints ADDED, DUPLICATE, 1.
input_format:
Line 1: the number of commands Q.
Next Q lines: one command each (see the description).
output_format: One output line for every ADD, HAS, COUNT and NAME command.
constraints:
1 <= Q <= 1000
-10^9 <= x, y <= 10^9 (integers)
Labels are words without spaces
hint_1: Without __hash__, defining __eq__ makes the class unhashable, so it cannot go in a set.
hint_2: Hashing the tuple (x, y) gives equal points equal hashes.
hint_3: Point(1, 2) in points calls __hash__ first, then __eq__ to confirm the match.

title: Fraction Arithmetic Dunders
objective: Implement __add__, __sub__, and __mul__ on Fraction with GCD reduction.
description:
Task: Write a class Frac for exact fractions (do not use the fractions module):
• __init__(self, num, den): if den is 0 raise ZeroDivisionError('zero denominator'). Store the fraction in lowest terms: divide both by math.gcd(num, den), and keep the sign in the numerator (the denominator is always positive)
• __add__, __sub__ and __mul__ each return a NEW Frac
a/b + c/d = (a*d + c*b) / (b*d), a/b - c/d = (a*d - c*b) / (b*d), a/b * c/d = (a*c) / (b*d)
• __str__ returns 'num/den', or just 'num' when den is 1

Each input line is one expression: <fraction> <op> <fraction>, where a fraction is written num/den and op is +, - or *. Print the result with str(). If creating a fraction raises ZeroDivisionError, print ERROR: zero denominator.

Examples: 1/2 + 1/3 → 5/6, 2/4 * 2/1 → 1, 1/0 + 1/2 → ERROR: zero denominator.
input_format:
Line 1: the number of expressions Q.
Next Q lines: <num>/<den> <op> <num>/<den>, separated by spaces.
output_format: Q lines: the result, or ERROR: zero denominator.
hint_1: math.gcd always returns a non-negative number; math.gcd(0, 5) is 5, so 0/5 becomes 0/1.
hint_2: If den < 0 after reducing, multiply both num and den by -1.
hint_3: a + b on two Frac objects calls a.__add__(b).

title: Property Decorator Validation
objective: Use @property and @setter to enforce validation on private attribute.
description:
Task: A property looks like a normal attribute from outside, but runs your code when it is read or assigned. That lets a class reject bad values.

Write a class Product:
• __init__(self, name, price) stores the name in a read-only property and assigns self.price = price, so the setter checks the starting price too

description:

title: Context Manager Dunders
objective: Implement __enter__ and __exit__ for resource acquisition and error suppression.
description:
Task: A with statement calls __enter__ when the block starts and __exit__ when it ends, even if the block raises an error. If __exit__ returns True, the error is suppressed (swallowed); otherwise it continues outward.

title: In-Memory Command Undo/Redo
objective: Implement Command pattern with .execute() and .undo() on text document.
description:
Task: In the Command pattern every change is an object that knows how to do AND undo itself. An editor keeps the done commands on an undo stack, and undone commands on a redo stack.

Write:
• class Document with self.text = ''
• class AppendCommand(doc, text): execute adds text to the end; undo removes it again
• class DeleteCommand(doc, n): execute removes the last n characters (or all of them if there are fewer) and REMEMBERS what it removed; undo puts that text back
• class Editor:
- run(command): command.execute(), push it on the undo stack and CLEAR the redo stack
- undo(): pop from the undo stack, call undo(), push on the redo stack. Returns False when there is nothing to undo
- redo(): pop from the redo stack, call execute() again, push on the undo stack. Returns False when there is nothing to redo

• APPEND text → the text is everything after 'APPEND ' (it may contain spaces); prints nothing
• DELETE n → prints nothing
• UNDO → prints nothing, or NOTHING TO UNDO
• REDO → prints nothing, or NOTHING TO REDO
• SHOW → print the text between square brackets, for example [hello world]

objective: Define __eq__ and __lt__ and let functools.total_ordering supply the rest.
description:
Task: functools.total_ordering fills in <=, > and >= when a class defines __eq__ and ONE ordering method such as __lt__.

• __init__(self, text) stores the text and a tuple of ints. Remove zeros at the END of the tuple, so 1.0 and 1.0.0 are the same version (but keep at least one part)

title: LRU Cache Container
objective: Build an LRU cache with __getitem__, __setitem__, __delitem__, __contains__ and __len__.
time_complexity: O(1) per command, O(N) per SHOW
description:
Task: A Least Recently Used (LRU) cache holds at most capacity items. When it is full and a new key arrives, it removes the item that was used longest ago.

Write a class LRUCache that behaves like a dictionary through magic methods. Store the items in a collections.OrderedDict, oldest first:
• __init__(self, capacity)
• __setitem__(self, key, value): store the value and mark the key as most recently used (move_to_end). If the cache now has more than capacity items, remove the oldest one (popitem(last=False)) and remember its key in self.last_evicted (otherwise set self.last_evicted = None)
• __getitem__(self, key): return the value and mark the key as most recently used. A missing key raises KeyError
• __delitem__(self, key): remove the key (KeyError if missing)
• __contains__(self, key): True/False, WITHOUT changing the order
• __len__(self): the number of items
• __repr__(self): LRUCache([key1, key2, ...]) with the keys from oldest to newest, written as a Python list

The first line gives the capacity. Commands:
• PUT key value → cache[key] = value, then print OK, or OK (evicted <key>)
• GET key → print cache[key], or MISS
• HAS key → print key in cache
• DEL key → del cache[key] and print OK, or MISS
• LEN → print len(cache)
• SHOW → print repr(cache)

Example with capacity 2: PUT a 1, PUT b 2, GET a, PUT c 3 prints OK, OK, 1, OK (evicted b). Reading a made b the oldest.
